speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The change and expansion are driven by two key factors.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: First, as our economy grows in size and sophistication, we need more talent from wider fields of expertise.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Every parent wants his child to do well and have meaningful careers.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Many want to go to university, but each dream is different.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We must have a system that best fulfils that.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The two are interdependent and act in a certain cycle.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As the economy deepened and expanded, it enabled more students to attain higher levels of education and secure good jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And a stronger pool of talent made us more competitive and fuelled further growth.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Because of that, since year 2000, the university cohort participation rate has increased progressively, in tandem with our economic development.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: At the same time, the talent emerging from our universities becomes increasingly more diverse.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, we have five autonomous universities (AUs) − NUS, NTU, SMU, the Singapore University of Technology and Design (SUTD) and the Singapore Institute of Technology (SIT).

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: SMU and SUTD were set up in 2000 and 2011 respectively.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: SIT was conferred AU status in 2014 to pioneer the applied pathway, for specialised fields in science and technology.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Throughout this development, the great majority, around 90% of graduates from AUs, continue to find jobs within six months of their graduation.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is not the case in many countries where there is severe graduate unemployment because of an over-supply of graduates.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: SUSS will be a unique AU, clearly differentiated from the existing AUs, adding further diversity and choice to our university landscape.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: SUSS is built on the foundation of an earlier partnership between the Ministry of Education (MOE) and the Singapore Institute of Management (SIM), a private society.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In 1992, MOE turned to SIM to help develop programmes that would offer its non-graduate teachers an opportunity to deepen their knowledge in their teaching subjects.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Open University Degree Programmes grew out of this MOE-SIM collaboration.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: SIM eventually established the SIM University in 2005 to deliver these part-time degree courses.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In 2012, the Government selected SIM University to develop full-time programmes under the applied pathway as well, in addition to its mainstay of part-time degree programmes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In 2013, it was selected to host the third law school in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It offered full-time degree programmes in human resource (HR) management, social work and other areas, and were distinguished by its modular and flexible structure and novel opportunities for learning by doing.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: From an intake of 200 in 2014, the university now takes in about 580 students and its numbers are still growing.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As an AU, SUSS will become a permanent fixture in our higher education landscape, and stand shoulder-to-shoulder with the other five AUs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Students will continue to enjoy substantial Government subsidies for the cost of their education in SUSS.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They will have access to Government-supported financial assistance schemes for those who require more help with the cost of their studies.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The pathway that SUSS provides will be clearly differentiated from the other AUs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: First, SUSS will be a champion of lifelong learning.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Since its inception in 2005, the university has been providing quality learning opportunities to adult learners.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: To date, it has produced over 27,000 graduates, many of whom are working adults who had to juggle their studies with other work and family commitments.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For this reason, the university has continually sought to improve the structure and delivery of its programmes, including leveraging information and communications technology (ICT), in order to better support working students.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It will continue to refine its teaching model as learner, industry and societal needs evolve.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: SUSS will also expand its programme offerings for adult learners.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It will work with SkillsFuture Singapore (SSG) and sector agencies to develop industry-relevant courses and create new content that will support the upgrading of our industries.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Second, SUSS will deliver programmes that have a strong social focus.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: SUSS will champion disciplines that positively impact society and its development.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Part of this is to build a strong niche in the social sciences, such as social work, early childhood education and HR management.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In addition, it will infuse the mission of social development into other disciplines.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is increasingly important, as we need to balance economic growth with social development, and globalisation with a strong sense of community and nationhood.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Hence, in SUSS' full-time programmes, there is a compulsory service learning component which requires students to initiate, conceptualise, and execute a social project and champion a cause.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is also why, as host of Singapore's third law school, SUSS focuses on criminal and family lawyers.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Third, SUSS will continue to develop the applied degree pathway.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In this regard, SUSS will complement SIT, each with its own domain focus.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There will be strong interlacing of theoretical knowledge with real-life application, and the two universities will strengthen the nexus between institution and industry.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As SUSS prepares to take its next steps forward, I would like to take this opportunity to acknowledge SIM for its role in establishing and supporting the development of the university over the past 12 years.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It will be a fitting legacy to the good work of SIM.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: SUSS, like our other AUs, will be governed by an Act of Parliament.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is to safeguard public interests and use of public funds.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The SUSS Bill thus aims to serve three key functions.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Third, it permits the Government to provide resources to SUSS and monitor the performance and finances of the institution in order to ensure accountability for the use of public funds.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Clause 3 sets out the function of SUSS, which includes conferring and awarding degrees, diplomas and certificates.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Clauses 5, 6 and 8 allow the Government to guide the strategic development of SUSS and to appoint, remove and replace members of the SUSS Board of Trustees and ensure moneys provided by Parliament to SUSS may only be applied or expended by SUSS based on its public mission spelt out by the Act.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Clauses 4 and 9 allow the Government to monitor the performance and finances of SUSS through an accountability framework, including scrutiny of the accounts and financial statements of SUSS.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Clause 12 provides for consequential amendments to the Private Education Act, Chapter 247A, to provide that the Act will not apply to SUSS.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It also amends the Legal Profession Act and Singapore Academy of Law Act, to replace the words "SIM University" with the "Singapore University of Social Sciences", and lastly, the SkillsFuture Singapore Agency Act to include SUSS in the list of universities.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In this regard, I would like to end my speech today with some comments on the meaning of a university education.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The issue of university cohort participation rate has received some attention in the past few days, arising from a panel discussion I participated in at the 47th St Gallen Symposium.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: First, degrees, like most things in life, can become obsolete.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We live in a world where information and knowledge can be googled and are available online.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Skills are what carry a premium now, and skills need to be honed throughout our lifetime.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, let us not be overly fixated with how many percentage of each young student cohort moves on to attend universities, because all of us, 100%, need to keep learning and deepening our skills throughout our lives.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The second point I would like to make is that degrees do not earn us a living, and do not make our dreams come true.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Our ability to keep pace with the changing needs of the economy is what helps us earn our keep.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is the dedicated pursuit of a discipline that makes dreams come true.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We must, however, recognise that because our dreams and aspirations are diverse, the needs of economy are diverse, the path for upgrading must also be diverse and multitudinous.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They should include academic upgrades, yes, but also applied qualifications, apprenticeships, industry certifications, modular and frequent skills acquisitions, overseas exposures or simply gaining work experience and making for yourself a name in the industry or in your respective fields.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It will truly be "unimaginative" to confine ourselves to university academic education as the only way to fulfil our full potential.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Last, degrees do not define us individually or as a society.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I believe most of us agree that we do not want a society that defines success as simply having a degree.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Our society needs to evolve, such that all occupations, crafts and trades, whether the skills are acquired through a degree education or not, are respected and recognised.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have come so far in uniting all segments of the society for a common purpose.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Let us all continue to do our part to underscore and spread the message of inclusiveness, unity, celebrating and embracing all manners of achievements and successes.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Deputy Speaker, with UniSIM set to become our newest and sixth AU, I think this is a great opportunity for us to chart a different learning experience for SUSS graduands.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As mentioned by the Minister, there will be a strong SkillsFuture focus and I suggest also that it means "the now" and "the later".

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It means that our graduates should meet the skill requirements of jobs, that is, now, but also be adaptable to learn how to meet changing workplace needs.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The alignment to SkillsFuture, as mentioned by the Minister earlier, is very closely to what we know about the brand that UniSIM currently carries.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is traditionally known for its focus on continuing education and training for adult learners.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many of the students enrolled in its programmes, continuing their education in a degree on a part-time basis, are all working adults.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And today, they have a good mix of young and old students who hail from diverse backgrounds, adding to a rich learning experience.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As a champion for lifelong leaning, I am glad the new AU will continue to retain its distinctive offering and stay relevant to working professionals as the university for lifelong learning.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Beyond that, I look forward to SUSS being closely aligned to our direction of providing Singaporeans with the opportunity to attain mastery of skills.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Working adults, having already had a taste of working life, will now better understand the skills gaps and needs at the workplace, and they are eager to hone their skills and competencies.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am very confident that the new university will be able to bridge that gap.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I agree that we need to inculcate a culture of lifelong learning amongst our students and help our workers pick up industry-relevant skills and transferrable skills.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The reason for doing so is to continue what they have learnt at the workplace so that they can re-learn and un-learn and learn new skills at SUSS.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On the academic field, I hope there will be a good representation of lecturers or guest speakers who are experts in their respective industries or respective fields so that the students can learn from the best, not just from lecturers, but also from industry practitioners.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The lecturers and speakers in the university should have the appropriate pedagogy on providing adult learners with authentic learner engagements and also the ability to integrate work experiences into the tertiary curriculum.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On a related note, I would like to declare my interest as an Executive Secretary of the Education Services Union.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As we transit UniSIM into an AU, we should also prepare the non-academic staff in the university for this transition.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In their new work environment, student engagements, requirements from MOE, there may be new yardsticks, new key performance indicators (KPIs).

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that the management will work closely with the union to ensure that the workers on the ground will be able to manage this transition without being impacted by the change.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These, I believe, are useful knowledge that graduands will find that the workplace strongly requires many of our students to possess.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Furthermore, I would also like to encourage the Ministry to consider working with SUSS to include corporate governance, cross cultural knowledge, business ethics and corporate sustainability as applicable knowledge that the workplace will require and, if these could be modules in the university, I believe it will be an advantage that SUSS will be able to possess.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Minister earlier mentioned that they will be working with the lecturers, SkillsFuture and sectoral representatives to ensure that the content will be relevant to the workplace.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am very confident that with this approach, there will be a competency-based system ensuring that the graduands stay updated, having possessed skills and knowledge that are required at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Deputy Speaker, in conclusion, I am confident that the learning in the new university can have a strong weightage assigned to relevance to the market and content with a strong emphasis on applied learning.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I agree with what the Minister mentioned earlier for us not to just look at cohort size going to the universities, let us also not look at how many percent find jobs, but rather, whether will they be able to meet job requirements not of today's but also for future needs.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Having a job today does not mean that you are ready with adaptable skills for the future.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, with the university's focus on lifelong learning, I am confident that SUSS will be able to enable our adult learners to find jobs for today as well as jobs for tomorrow.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This reorientation will not just become a major milestone in our higher education field, but it will also have important consequences for Singapore society, as social science knowledge is brought to bear directly on the changing and increasingly complex social landscape.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While I support the Bill, I would like to raise four issues regarding the development of applied social sciences in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The first issue is the balancing of academic and applied social sciences.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Academic social sciences tend to be highly specialised, with the individual disciplines developing their own lineage of knowledge traditions and research methodologies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Academic social sciences are also more concerned with producing new theoretical knowledge of cause-and-effect.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Practical solutions and policy implications are secondary concerns.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Applied social sciences invert the emphases of academic social sciences.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Applied social sciences are multidisciplinary in structure and interdisciplinary in approach, with the focus on applying existing knowledge to understand specific social problems and develop practical solutions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Academic and applied social sciences need each other to do their work.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Applications of theoretical knowledge validate and vindicate the knowledge and will show up gaps that become the puzzles to push the research frontier.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Academic social sciences not only provide the theoretical knowledge for applied social scientists to work with, but also the tools of critical analysis for the scientists to evaluate solutions and policies in objective light.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To be effective, applied social sciences must be relevant to both academic social scientists and policymakers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is a need to balance academic and applied social sciences in the university, even if the university should focus on applied social sciences.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As paradoxical as this may sound, I urge the Minister to safeguard the autonomy of the applied social scientists from policymakers, even as we seek greater relevance of social research to social policy and ensure the balance of academic and applied social sciences in SUSS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With this sixth AU, Singapore will have an enhanced and diverse higher education field.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But a closer look at the diversity reveals yet another risk.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The three older universities, that is, NUS, NTU and SMU, are academic in orientation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is also a division of labour among them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: NUS has the full suite of academic disciplines and more, with cutting-edge residential and liberal arts colleges in University Town.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: NTU is focused on the technological sciences, while SMU specialises in management sciences.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The three newer universities, that is, SUTD, SIT and now SUSS, offer applied learning.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is also a division of labour among them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: SUTD focuses on application of design to technological innovation, SIT specialises in applied learning in the industries and SUSS zooms in on applied social sciences.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is a discomforting symmetry in this diversity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Already as such, in NUS, I am a lot more networked with international scholars than I am with my peers in the other five universities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In developed economies with advanced tertiary education sectors, there is a balance between competition and complementation among the universities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A highly differentiated university sector means that the universities will appear to complement one another at the highest level of planning for the education of our workforce and compete for the same pot of research funding.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, the departments and research centres in each university will have little incentive to interact and network with their counterparts in other universities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There will be little competition of ideas, which is what makes for a thriving university sector.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This problem of becoming a silo university will affect SUSS more because its subject focus is the social landscape in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Let us take the institution of the family as an example.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is no longer tenable in sociology to speak of a single form of family, that is, the modern nuclear family underpinned by marriage and functionally set up for making and growing babies to become good citizens.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Individual choices, new forms of partnership, new ways of childbearing and childrearing, dissolutions of marriages have led to a plurality of families and complex new social problems.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In such a complex social landscape, applied social sciences have to take the lead in research and knowledge production, and the nature of this leadership has to be different from that of academic social sciences.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The theoretical knowledge offered by academic social sciences is no longer adequate in themselves, and its insularity from society means that academic social scientists are likely to be unaware of the emerging trends in the social landscape.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But for applied social scientists to take the lead, SUSS would need to be highly networked with communities in the social field, and the knowledge production must reside in the relationship between the university and the communities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In academic social sciences, the research problems and analyses take place in the university, and the social field matters only as the site where data is collected to be brought back into the university.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Applied social sciences work with communities to define research problems and data, and analyses are often generated in collaboration with community partners.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Results of the research are not just published as findings but are applied as practical solutions to be continuously evaluated.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The risk, again, of setting up an entire university dedicated to applied social sciences is that the university will see itself and be seen by the Government and society as the centre of expert knowledge about social problems.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Applied social sciences have had many decades of development in Anglo-American universities, and one of the problems that have been identified is precisely this problem of applied social sciences becoming too academic and losing its community grounding.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One of the ways to mitigate this is for the university to work with community partners to set up community-based research centres.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This would necessitate at least two changes to the structure of research funding.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The administration of these grants would have to be more flexible and adapted to specific needs on the ground.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The fourth issue is less institutional and more about the quality of the social scientists who staff the teaching positions and drive the research work.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I believe that we need to prioritise quality first and foremost over other considerations, including the question of nationality that has come up in this House before.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What Singaporeans deserve are the best professors in the world to teach them to become the best social scientists they can be and to conduct the most cutting-edge research to help solve our social problems.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Decades of experience of applied social science research in Anglo-American universities show that immigrant and local-born professors perform equally well.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Nationality matters insofar as there would be a natural commitment on the part of Singaporean professors to the country and society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On the quality of our social scientists, especially with regard to growing a critical mass of excelling Singaporean social scientists, the Government can help by supporting the setting up of an Academy of Social Sciences and disciplinary associations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Presently, the ecosystem connecting locally based social scientists is very weak.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The dearth of associational life has driven many of us to join the national associations of other countries, for example, for me, the American Sociological Association.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We also need an academy as our representative body to advance the governance and standards of research and teaching in the social sciences.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The establishment of SUSS presents us with a good opportunity to grow the intellectual ecosystem for social science.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Beyond these four issues, I have a more immediate practical matter to bring up.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The question that some SIM University alumni have with the metamorphosis of their alma mater to SUSS is whether their certificates could be reprinted under the SUSS banner.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some have argued that this should not be, as education in SUSS would be of a higher quality than in SIM University, and thus it would be an unfair upgrade for the alumni.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is a view that seems to echo the popular stereotype and condescension of SIM University as inferior.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is precisely because of such popular myths that we should not unfairly stigmatise SIM University alumni.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Already, the change to SUSS is being read as an upgrade from an inferior species to a superior creature.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Without the hungry caterpillar, there would not be a beautiful butterfly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should not deny the contribution of SIM University alumni to the making of SUSS and deprive SUSS of that important history and a body of proud alumni.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The one most important single line that connects SIM University and SUSS is the emphasis on lifelong learning.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, this Bill marks a new chapter for our higher education sector and a new era for social scientists to contribute their knowledge making to the betterment of society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have raised four issues with the unprecedented establishment of an entire university dedicated to applied social sciences.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I sincerely hope that we will successfully navigate these issues and come out on the winning side, which would be a big win for Singapore society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I also hope that we would do the right thing for the SIM University alumni who have done their part in the making of SUSS.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is a good decision on three counts.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: One, there is no other university in Singapore that currently occupies and claims that unique domain space of the applied social sciences.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: As Singapore's social demographics change and the needs and demands in society become graver and more challenging, the need for more in-depth analyses and application of social science studies becomes correspondingly very critical.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The second reason why SUSS is a good decision is this.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: UniSIM was a private school with a known brand and history of more than 20 years.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The Government's support of this private university will help fulfil its promise to create more university places in the public education space.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This is a promise that was made when Minister Lawrence Wong was then helming the tertiary education space in MOE.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: SUSS will, indeed, help meet the brewing aspirations of many fresh undergraduates and working adults to get a first degree.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But the most important reason why this Bill reflects a good decision is this.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: UniSIM's, and now SUSS', unique experience of primarily catering to busy working adults pursuing further studies falls squarely in place with Singapore's SkillsFuture movement.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Our SkillsFuture movement is an important shift which encourages lifelong learning and skills mastery, and it features a very important type of education for our future economy.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Perhaps less known to the public is the fact that SUSS, then UniSIM, is a forerunner in the provision of e-learning in the Singapore tertiary space.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Even before other universities jumped on the bandwagon of digital education, before the term "online learning" became a mantra, the former UniSIM had been investing in and learning the business of e-learning and blending it with face-to-face class interactions.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The purpose was to deliver programmes anytime, anywhere, on any personal data assistant (PDA), via multimedia channels and blended learning, to meet the demanding schedules of its busy adult learners.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: At a time when most tertiary institutions are doing the catch-up on online and blended learning, SUSS is already way ahead in digital education and catering to an adult learner population in a fast-paced work setting.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Clause 3 sets out the function of the university company.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Clause 8 provides for Parliament to give funding and requires that the moneys given may only be applied for such objects.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, I would like to be assured by the Minister in three specific areas so that SUSS would not end up becoming just like another ordinary university, losing its edge and the opportunity to help put Singapore on the map of future learning.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The first is to do with positioning, SUSS' positioning, both in terms of what it offers and who the target learners are.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Whilst Social Science is an appealing focus, a search online would reveal that branches of Social Science can cover a full spectrum from anthropology, education, social work, business studies, economics, political science, psychology to sustainability studies.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But at the same time, to add to the complication, there are also talks amongst many education experts that there is a need, like what Assoc Prof Daniel Goh said, to ensure that subjects are not taught in silos.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There is a real need to blend some of the subjects, and that is what many educators are talking about.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I, therefore, would like to seek the Minister's views on the long-term positioning of a university, such as SUSS.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In addition, if SUSS is to provide lifelong learning programmes for adults, I seek the Minister's clarification on what "adult learners" actually are.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Although this is older than the 19-year-olds who normally enter the other universities, how would SUSS cater to working adults who are much older and, especially, those who decide to take up new skills or a new second or third career?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In a world where old jobs disappear and future jobs requiring new skills emerge, is there an intent for MOE to give these older learners more than one bite of the cherry in their pursuit of tertiary studies?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Can they pursue several tertiary level courses throughout their lifetime?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: My second query is in the area of resourcing and funding.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: SUSS will need to be sufficiently resourced to allow it to acquire the faculty to deepen the disciplinary focus of social sciences and to conduct applied research in the social sciences.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In addition, there is a great opportunity to further propel the SUSS' traditional strength in online and blended learning.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: SUSS can become a regional or global lead in not just a provider of digital education for adult learners but also a provider of expert services, consultancy in education technology and design.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Whilst the entrepreneurial and nimble spirit of SUSS should never be lost, the new AU must receive funding support that allows it to delve deeper into its social science domain and also not to lose its traditional strength.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: My third concern is on how a university like SUSS would be evaluated by the Ministry, the Government, its learners and also the public.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The commonly held success criteria by which universities are gauged include the popular ranking systems, such as research robustness, publications in journals and the like.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Tertiary education enrolment in Singapore has been expanding continuously over the last few decades.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This expansion has been driven by the rising educational aspirations of Singaporeans and made possible by increasing Government expenditures on education.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: From 2000 to 2015, total expenditure slowed as development expenditure on education plateaued.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Despite that, total expenditure still grew by 110% in those years, driven by recurrent expenditures.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: University-level education has consistently taken up the bulk of this in aggregate terms.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In international terms, even though Singapore does not spend the most, it compares favourably with other economies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: However, we should also note that it was below Brazil's, New Zealand's, Malaysia's as well as those of most of the Nordic states.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In 2000, 33,298 resident students were attending university.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This manifold increase in university enrolment numbers emphatically underlines the growing desire for degree qualifications.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: To accommodate such strong growth in enrolment, the Government has promoted measures aimed at strengthening governance while encouraging innovation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The SMU Corporatisation Bill was also passed at the same Sitting.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In 2012, the Prime Minister announced that the number of universities in Singapore would be increased to six, with the addition of SIT and UniSIM.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: These are all part of the Government's fulfilment of its commitment to achieve targeted increases in the proportion of each cohort which would earn tertiary educational qualifications.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: With the renaming of UniSIM as SUSS, and its inclusion among the AUs overseen by MOE, Singaporeans have an even greater range of options to choose from when deciding on further education.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: More tertiary students are taking up internships and overseas exchanges than ever before, reflecting the growing industry focus and international outlook of our Institutions of Higher Learning (IHLs).

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, technology is changing the landscape of education altogether.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Learning is less tied to physical location than ever before.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Virtual learning models, such as massive open online courses and flipped classrooms, are rendering previously recognised boundaries of instructor-student interaction obsolete.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: For SUSS, which has carved a place out as the only private university in Singapore's higher education landscape, this Bill represents a very significant milestone.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The change enacted by this Bill is coming under greater MOE oversight.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In contrast, when NUS and NTU made the change to AUs from being Statutory Boards, they were moving to less Government scrutiny.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, even as a private university, SUSS has been enjoying strong support from the Government since its inception.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: There is no doubt in my mind that greater support from the Government will enable SUSS to do even more for its students.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In particular, I would like to emphasise the importance of catering to the needs of working adults who wish to take up degree studies without leaving the workforce.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: I would just like to ask for some clarifications about the direction of funding and support for working adults going forward.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, during the Debate on the President's Address in 2011, Mr Ang Wei Neng asked about the difference between the subsidy rates for part-time and full-time degree programmes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: If one looks at the fees payable for any particular programme, say, accountancy, in any of the AUs, the total fees for part-time programmes could be lower than those for their full-time counterparts in many cases.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Minister clarify the bases upon which these rates should be interpreted?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Another question I have related to this is about working adults wanting to enrol in university courses and their eligibility then for financial assistance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Despite this, publicly-funded tertiary education in Singapore still represents a significant cost to low-income families.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In its commitment to ensure that all deserving students are given a chance to achieve tertiary education, the Government as well as other organisations offer a range of schemes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: These include bursaries, loans and scholarships, and are meant "to cover not only the remaining tuition fees payable but also to help students defray their costs of living".

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: But I would like to ask the Minister how, if such students are working, whether their personal incomes are taken into account in assessing their eligibility for loans, bursaries or other schemes which could help to reduce the financial burden of tuition fees.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: If the student were the main breadwinner of a family, say, was considering pursuing a degree, would his or her application for financial assistance be assessed similarly as those who are still mainly dependent on their parents for financial support?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In closing, please let me talk about this, based on my personal observations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: From personal experience, I have found that all working adults take their academic studies very seriously even under the pressure of job deadlines.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, unlike most full-time students who are not yet working, working adults have to bear the strain of competing priorities from their jobs as well as their family commitments.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: And the Minister kindly alluded to this in his earlier remarks.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: For each student who works and studies at the same time, there is an individual story of perseverance and dedication.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In each and every case, the journey they embark upon is a joint endeavour made through the combined support of their employers, their loved ones and their fellow students.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Unlike students in full-time programmes who can easily participate in extracurricular activities during breaks from schoolwork, working adults have to juggle multiple roles that leave them little time to pursue similar interests.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: It is not uncommon to see students rushing into classes at night after having come straight from their workplaces without having taken dinner yet and then hurrying back home to attend to their family commitments once classes end.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The diversity of experiences will stand both groups in good stead and deepen their insight into the resilience of our students and workers and bind them in a shared learning journey.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: I would just like to recall three comments in conclusion that relate to this change which has left a deep impression on me personally, and which I feel best give voice to my feelings.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: First, I had the opportunity to get the thoughts of Prof Cheong Hee Kiat, President of SUSS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: I would just like to paraphrase what he told me as follows: "with what we have done as UniSIM and in what SUSS will do in the future through its various pathways and educational modalities, lifelong learning is promoted and opportunities expanded for various groups of people.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: But as we expand these opportunities, more learners with a wide spread of abilities will take courses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: We want to help them learn effectively and find joy and satisfaction in learning.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: That means more support for learners will be needed." I strongly empathise with his concerns about the need to focus on the diverse needs of different groups of learners.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Second, while thinking about the weight of the responsibility that SUSS carries, I cannot help but be struck by one particular remark that Prof Aline Wong, Chancellor of SUSS, made at our recent 12th Anniversary Celebration Lunch last month.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: She reminded us that the mantle of being SUSS has a special significance at this point of our nation's development, as we witness around us a burgeoning interest in social science phenomena, both global and local, ranging from the popular to the esoteric.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Her point, I believe, is that, as a university, we must continue to strive uncompromisingly for academic excellence in advancing the social sciences as a rigorous discipline.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In an age of rapid technological disruption, the social sciences have an added relevance as they explore the impact of change on society as well as the possible solutions to its problems, new and old.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: This includes methods for coping with the impact, from the point of view of not just economic outcomes, such as employment, but also psychological outcomes, such as individual and familial well-being, and sociological outcomes, such as those arising out of the spread of social media influence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: In closing, I would like to recall Minister Ong Ye Kung's speech at SUSS' Convocation Ceremony in October last year.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Minister Ong again also referred to the same thing earlier in his opening when he recounted UniSIM's history and the role played by SIM in its development.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: His words remind me of the tremendous support SUSS has received to reach this stage.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: His words spoke to my own experience, too, for, as someone who worked alongside and personally benefited from the support, advice and friendship of colleagues from the various departments of the SIM Group, I fondly recall their kindness and collegiality.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Social science is a very broad-spectrum term and really, as some of them say, even medicine is a social science on a grand scale.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: In this context, can the Minister update us on the migration process as well as the support rendered in this direction?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Will there be any major changes or revamp that we will see, especially pertaining to the governance structure, the educators and also, I assume, a proportion of them will be retained and also developed?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Thirdly, also being a public university, we now know that the students there will be subjected to receiving tertiary support from all the various sources that are available to students from other universities as well.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: I have a concern pertaining to the adult learners who are enrolled at this university because they may not be applicable to receive some of the funding support that may be applicable to the full-time students.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Therefore, perhaps it will be good at this point in time and also at this juncture of development of Singapore to see how we can help support adult learning so that they can continue lifelong learning and also to learn, unlearn and relearn, which is really an important mantra in the world of today's business.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Fourthly, UniSIM has had a strong culture and outlook in service learning and exposures for students, including both local as well as overseas experiential learning and project work.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: I hope that this will be retained and perhaps even developed and enhanced even further with collaboration and partnership with the other AUs in Singapore and overseas as well.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This, according to many, has injected some level of flexibility into the curriculum and also the payment structure.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: It is relevant and quite a proportion of the students who are adult learners are actually tapping on the scheme.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This is slightly different form other universities where payment and fees are done by the number of years or semesters a student is in the school, for example.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Thus, for SUSS now, which model is going to be utilised and, better still, if we can have a hybrid model so that there is more flexibility for our adult learners?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: But it is really what the holder of the degree can do, will do or is willing to do.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: If he can learn, unlearn and relearn and make himself relevant to industry, to the practice of his industry and business, then that is what we really want.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: If I may ask the Minister, in conjunction with SkillsFuture as well as the need to develop a dual education track, will the new SUSS consider a professional development academy?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: This would be in addition to the Academy of Social Sciences that my Parliamentary colleague referred to earlier.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: This would be focused on the professional skills.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: This is something that is similarly done currently, in conferring both certificates and Masters qualifications at NUS, NTU and SMU.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps, SUSS could also consider doing so as well.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: My second question would be, within social sciences, what is the niche that SUSS wishes to occupy, keeping a firm eye on the job market?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: When we actually produce students within SUSS, what are the disciplines that they would be occupying and working in?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: When we say applied social sciences, what are the jobs that we are thinking of?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Put differently, what is the specific strategic development model and external collaborations that the Ministry has in mind for SUSS?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: If we were to think of NUS as either a Yale or Harvard, SUTD and SIT as MIT of Singapore, SMU as Wharton or the University of London, what would be SUSS' comparator?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: What would be the model that we would use?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: And how much cross-AU collaborations would we find?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I would add my voice to what was raised earlier by Assoc Prof Daniel Goh when he said that there is not that much cross-AU collaborations or even intra-university collaborations but there is a lot of inter-university collaborations between Singapore universities and international universities.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Is SUSS going to be perhaps a dynamo of inter-university collaborations within Singapore using professional development and continuing lifelong learning as the basis to do so?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: When we think about social development, that is the core focus of SUSS.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Would the projects that are being proposed by the academics within the university be in collaboration with the Government agencies or would we be able to see projects that are also being proposed in collaboration with businesses as well, in terms of social development?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: If that is anything to go by for the third law school at SUSS, we are going to be in for a treat.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is good that we give focus on producing graduates in social work and early childhood education, which are areas where there is a need to shore up our pool of trained manpower in this area.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am also pleased that the university will also be running courses to produce graduates in HR management.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Social science, as we know, and most of the speakers have mentioned, is known as a very broad subject on the scientific study of human society and social relationships.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Sometimes, the word "social science" conjures up an image of people working in a social work or teaching environment only.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, the roles available within this discipline is, in fact, very wide as well as focusing on a wide range of issues.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Hopefully, with the training of more social scientists, we can overcome societal issues in Singapore and build stronger ties.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This would be particularly helpful if such programmes can be run on a part-time basis, as I believe many of them would be working adults.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Speaking of relationships, it is equally important that we also produce graduates who are specialised in the area of HR.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With so much being said about quality of life, finding a balance between productivity and rewards and, in times when the various sectors are facing headwinds resulting in staff downsizing, good and competent HR practitioners are important to handle such issues sensitively and advise management on how to bridge gaps between employers and the unions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Institute has a treasure trove of information and historical archives that would do well to help students in understanding the tripartite relations in Singapore's society.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Perhaps the Minister can share if there are plans for the university to expand more courses relating to criminology and forensic psychology studies so that our law enforcement officers can better equip themselves for the challenges ahead.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We can strive to be the regional centre for such studies on terrorism and related subjects and complement the courses run by the Rajaratnam School of International Studies.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One area of focus which I hope the curriculum would look into is how to get families to break the silence.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Often, the victims suffer in silence for many years before they open up.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, there must be some training in counselling to get the victims to open up.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We have been expanding fast in setting up childcare centres throughout the island.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While the physical infrastructure is important, so, too, is the quality of the people who run these centres.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These childhood educators are very important for they are planting and caring for the seeds that will eventually germinate to become the youths and the adults in our society.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must not look at our childhood educators as the kindergarten teachers in the old days, in the 1950s and 1960s.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Will SUSS put emphasis on research in the local context?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There should be more research done on childhood education so that we can have a good repository of knowledge.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Understanding the mindset of the child, understanding how their young minds receive and process information, and what are best ways to help them absorb information are areas where we should look into.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This should not be constrained just to childhood education, in my view, in SUSS, but also other social science subject in SUSS, including frontier studies or research on domestic and economic issues and policy implications and possible partnerships with the economic agencies in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I hope as we strive for a high standard in our universities, we will not impose too high criteria for entry to the various programmes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Yes, we want quality students but we should balance this with aptitude.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is a waste of public funds if the people who graduate do not make use of their qualifications to practise but instead take jobs unrelated to their training.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Lastly, I believe that, in time, SUSS would be working on exchange programmes with other universities abroad so that students can also benefit from cross-fertilisation of ideas with their counterparts from other cultures.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Also, it should look into getting learning attachments abroad to give students better exposure.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What is happening right now is they often turn to their parents for help to get good attachments with companies abroad.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The success rate, I believe, is only a small percentage.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The new SUSS' focus on adult learners is important and timely.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Workers will have more opportunities to broaden or deepen their knowledge.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I support SUSS' move to integrate applied learning into its curriculum.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It also improves speed to market for our graduates.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is a step in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In fact, this could contribute towards the continuous need to close the skills gap of our workers, an issue which was highlighted by our Manpower Minister recently.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How does this fit in with the focus on social sciences and how will its graduates differentiate themselves from those who take similar programmes in other universities?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: As SUSS is the only one of the six universities with a stronger focus on adult learners, how would the university work with the industry to improve the employability of students?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How will SUSS work with the industry, Labour Movement or Workforce Singapore (WSG) to ensure that students who wish to switch careers or advance their careers are given proper support and network with employers in their field of study?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Would they also similarly have structured access to internships and attachments in the industry?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But what if industry and social demands change in the future?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, with the lower birth rates, the need for early childhood specialists may not be as high as it is now.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How will SUSS ensure that its programmes are sustainable in the long term?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In addition, I believe that for continued relevance and productivity, the strong social focus of the programmes must be infused by the best that digital and technological developments can offer.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The investment in disciplines with a strong social focus is important as it underpins a Singapore that is transforming its economy and societal fabric.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The focus on adult and lifelong learning can accelerate developing new ways of keeping our workforce nimble and relevant.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It has also been increasing the number of course offerings, both for undergraduates and lifelong learners.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These are encouraging signs that since UniSIM's humble beginnings as a small private university, it has only been growing from strength to strength.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This new Bill will give it a further boost, and the new SUSS will definitely benefit from additional funding from MOE.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Mr Toh said and I quote, "I am fine with its new name in English.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As for its Chinese name, please use '新 加 坡 社 会 科 学 大 学 ', or '新 社 科 大 ' in short. '新 跃 社 会 科 学 大学 ' sounds odd although I think their intention is to keep the word '新 跃.'".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I believe that while a name could seem like a trivial matter, it ultimately carries the identity of the school, especially as it aspires towards global ambitions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Thus, it is something we should give careful consideration to, and I hope that the Minister will consider this name change.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, UniSIM currently offers a long list of degrees outside of the social sciences, including business, science and technology, as the Member has previously said.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There is some feedback about the new English name of the university as well.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify why it will be called the University of Social Sciences which seems to ignore the fact that it offers courses outside of social sciences?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If there are, indeed, changes, could I ask what are the factors in deciding to drop these programmes and whether there will be sufficient places at other universities for students intending to pursue them?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will there also be any staff members affected by the change?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For example, are there plans to retain or transfer the staff members for degree programmes that are dropped, to other universities?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I strongly support this move as Singapore's needs in the social sector continue to increase.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, as much as the new SUSS can differentiate itself through its niche course offerings and flexible course arrangements, universities are ultimately pitted side by side through global rankings, and this is how they "compete" for the best applicants.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We know that UniSIM is not yet on par with NUS, NTU and SMU.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Just looking at one well-recognised ranking, for example, QS World University Rankings, UniSIM does not feature on their list.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I suspect that a top GCE "A" level student passionate about family law may still choose to study at the more prestigious law school at NUS.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Of course, this will take some time, but as the new SUSS receives additional support from MOE, what are its plans to boost its reputation and quality of education?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For example, will it be reaching out to well-respected academics to join as faculty members?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The addition of a new AU will better serve our younger population, adult learners and help Singapore to strengthen its position as an educational hub.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As such, I stand in support of this Bill.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, the restructuring and rebranding of UniSIM to SUSS to reflect its focus on social sciences are a highly commendable move.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: It demonstrates the increasing relevance and importance of the study of social sciences and the format of education.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: In a recent media interview, the hon Minister for Higher Education and Skills, Mr Ong Ye Kung, very eloquently put it, "The name was chosen to reflect the university's mission of driving lifelong learning anchored in disciplines with a strong social focus." I very much support this Bill which provides huge opportunities for adult learners to pursue an applied education in the social sciences.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: It also speaks of the importance of analytical and critical thinking skills and would provide a more holistic view in policy planning and research.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I shall now touch on the name change.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: As mentioned by Mr Louis Ng, many Singaporeans do welcome this change.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps, the university could have been given a more neutral name and yet clearly represent the essence, substance and flavour of social sciences.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There are many suggestions for SUSS −more professional development programmes, forming an academy, inter-university collaborations, collaborations with industries, research direction.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: All these paint a very exciting picture and future for the SUSS team.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It will be an exciting and busy time for them ahead.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: All these we will take in while we plan out what they will do for the future.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The whole intention is to raise SUSS to a much more prestigious level and bring social sciences and social development courses to a much higher level in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In this whole process, SUSS, I think, will get busier, it will expand, it will not contract.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This actually is the most important aspect of this exercise.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I mentioned earlier that SUSS is a unique AU in three ways.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: First, it has a strong social focus; second, applied learning; third, lifelong learning.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: On the focus on social sciences, Mr Desmond Choo asked if the discipline is sustainable in the long run.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think this is not something we need to worry about.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So long as the Singapore economy remains diverse and vibrant, it will need talents of all kinds.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As an illustration, today, successful tech companies do not just hire coders and engineers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They are hiring anthropologists, psychologists and other social scientists as well.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Desmond Choo, Mr Louis Ng and Ms Thanaletchimi also asked if business and engineering programmes at SUSS would be disadvantaged because of its new name.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The naming and the actual courses in a university are never neat.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That is the reality here as well as all over the world.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If we look across the university landscape, NTU also offers arts and social science disciplines; London School of Economics also offers law, international relations and accountancy; SMU offers IT courses.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is, hence, common for universities to offer quality programmes beyond what their names imply.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The term "Social Sciences" in the name of SUSS thus reflects more than just social science disciplines that the university will build, but also its approach to incorporate a social focus in all its other disciplines.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I hope that by restructuring SUSS into an AU, we can raise the prestige of all graduates, past and present, across all disciplines.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: SUSS will broaden its range of offerings, as suggested by Mr Ang Hin Kee and also Mr Saktiandi Supaat, and we can grow the prestige of the discipline, as suggested by Assoc Prof Daniel Goh.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And since we are on the topic of its name, let me address Ms Thanaletchimi's question about whether we can have a generic name rather than "SUSS" referring to Social Sciences.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I went online and checked out the definition of SUSS − "suss" as a verb, means to realise or grasp; as a noun, it refers to knowledge and awareness of a specified kind; and, as an adjective, it means shrewd and wary.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, I think the Board of Trustees of SUSS had all these generic qualities in mind when they decided on the name, and it applies to all disciplines.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Louis Ng also raised a question about SUSS' name in Chinese.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The issue of name is one of the hardest things to settle.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The full Chinese name, as he pointed out, is “新跃社科大学”.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, it is not so easy to change.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The university went through much deliberation and decided on this name rather than "新加坡社科大学", which is a direct translation of SUSS.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Why “新跃”, the first two words, is really because “新跃” was in SIM University's Chinese name for many years.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As we restructure it, it would be good to recognise the legacy of SIM University and retain the words “新跃”.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I know that a name is always subjective.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
